Using the Equations to Trade Profitably

Which equations still matter, and how they turn into money in practice. Formulas are in trading_equations.md (numbers like "eq 6" refer to it). Education, not investment advice.

The core idea

No equation finds profits by itself. Profit comes from an edge: a repeatable pattern that pays more than it costs. The equations do three jobs around that edge:

  1. Prove the edge is real after costs, and bigger than just holding the Nifty.
  2. Size positions so you survive the bad runs and let the edge compound.
  3. Control risk with stops, time limits and kill switches when the edge fades.

Most retail traders lose on #1 (no edge after costs) or #2 (betting too big). SEBI's data says 87–93% of F&O traders lose money (../../../projects/trading experiments/indian_market_strategies_research.md).

Which equations still matter

EquationStill matters?How it makes or saves money
Expectancy (eq 1)EssentialTells you if a strategy makes money per trade after costs. Negative → stop, no matter how good it looks
Sharpe / Sortino (eq 2–3)EssentialCompares strategies fairly. Below buy-and-hold Nifty → just buy the index
Max drawdown (eq 4)EssentialDecides if you can stick with it, and when to switch a strategy off
CAPM alpha/beta (eq 5)YesShows whether profit is skill (alpha) or just a leveraged bet on the market (beta)
Kelly / Merton (eq 6–7)Yes, as a ceilingUpper limit on bet size. Use ≤ ¼ of it
Fixed-fractional size (eq 8)EssentialTurns "risk 1%" into an exact share count; the main thing that keeps accounts alive
Vol targeting (eq 9)YesEqual risk per position; what professional trend-following funds use
ATR (eq 10)EssentialStops that adapt to how much a stock normally moves
Annualised vol / GARCH (eq 11–12)YesCut size when volatility spikes, before the big losses
Black–Scholes / expected move (eq 13–14)Only for F&ORead IV, compare IV with realised volatility, know your Greeks
OU + z-score (eq 15–16)YesPairs trading: a market-neutral edge that doesn't need a direction call
HMM regimes (eq 17)OptionalTurn strategies on or off by market regime
Almgren–Chriss, Avellaneda–Stoikov (eq 18–19)Not for retailNeed large orders, tick data and fast infrastructure

The workflow: from idea to live trading

Step 1 — Start from a known source of edge

Edges with research behind them (see the research file above):

  • Momentum / trend: stocks that rose over 6–12 months tend to keep rising. This and quality/low-vol factors have the strongest evidence in Indian equities.
  • Mean reversion between related stocks: pairs trading (eq 15–16).
  • Volatility risk premium: option IV is usually above the volatility that actually happens, so option sellers earn a premium on average. They also take rare, large losses, so it needs strict sizing.

Single-indicator rules (RSI/MACD crossovers) have weak evidence. My own backtests found the same.

Step 2 — Backtest and apply pass/fail tests

Run the backtest with real costs and slippage, then check:

TestEquationPass if
Edge after costsExpectancy> 0 R per trade, over at least ~100 trades
Better than the index?Sharpe vs Nifty buy-and-holdHigher Sharpe, or low correlation to the index
Skill vs marketAlpha, betaAlpha > 0; beta isn't doing all the work
SurvivableMax drawdownA drawdown 1.5–2× the backtest's would still be bearable
RobustSame statsPositive on most symbols and on data the rules weren't tuned on (out-of-sample)

If it fails any test, don't trade it. That decision alone saves most of the money retail traders lose.

Step 3 — Size every trade

  1. Choose risk per trade: 0.5–1% of capital (eq 8).
  2. Place the stop by volatility: e.g. 2 × ATR from entry (eq 10).
  3. Quantity = (capital × risk%) ÷ (entry − stop).
  4. Check against Kelly (eq 6): never risk more than ¼ of full Kelly.
  5. Across a portfolio, scale each position so they carry similar volatility (eq 9), and cut size when GARCH/realised volatility jumps (eq 12).

Step 4 — Manage the trade

  • Exit at the stop or target, with no exceptions.
  • Mean-reversion trades get a time stop of 2–3 OU half-lives (eq 16).
  • Optional: only trade a trend strategy when an HMM says the market is trending (eq 17).

Step 5 — Monitor live and switch off when broken

  • Track rolling expectancy and Sharpe over the last 30–50 trades.
  • Kill switch: stop trading the strategy if the live drawdown passes 1.5–2× the backtested maximum, or expectancy turns negative over a meaningful sample. Edges fade; this catches it.

Why sizing matters more than the entry signal (simulation)

Setup from my best backtest: daily trendline Break, 51.5% win rate, 2R target, with 0.1R cost per trade. 20,000 simulated paths of 200 trades each. The second and third blocks show what happens if the true win rate is lower than the backtest says, which is common.

True win rate (expectancy after cost)Risk per tradeMedian end (× start)Chance of a ≥ 50% drawdownChance of losing 90%
51.5% (+0.45R)1%2.4×0%0%
2%5.4×0%0%
6.8% (¼ Kelly)145×39%0%
27.3% (full Kelly)huge100%3%
45% (+0.25R)1%1.6×0%0%
2%2.5×0.2%0%
6.8%10.9×79%0.1%
27.3%0.19×100%47%
36% (−0.02R, no real edge)1%0.94×0.2%0%
2%0.85×25%0%
6.8%0.30×99.5%21%
27.3%~0×100%99%

What it shows:

  • At 1–2% risk you survive every case, including the one where the edge turns out to be zero.
  • Big sizing only looks good if the backtest's win rate is exactly right. If it's a few points lower, the same sizing turns a good strategy into a likely wipe-out.
  • The large multipliers assume the edge stays constant for 200 trades with independent outcomes. Real edges decay and losses cluster, so real results are much lower. Read the table for the drawdown and ruin columns, not as a profit forecast.

Applied to my backtests (projects/trading experiments/)

  • SuperTrend + DI: expectancy turned negative after charges → fails Step 2. Don't trade it.
  • MACD + RSI + Stoch: negative on 5m; the daily version with the "MACD crosses down" exit had profit factor ~1.5–1.7 after delivery costs → worth adding Sharpe, drawdown and an out-of-sample test.
  • Tori trendline Break (daily): positive on 13/13 symbols but rarely beat buy-and-hold → Sharpe/alpha vs Nifty is the deciding test. If alpha ≈ 0, an index fund does the same job with less work.
  • Next experiments worth running: a momentum portfolio with vol-targeted sizing, and a cointegrated pairs strategy with OU-based exits. These rely on edges with more evidence than indicator crossovers.
